newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ready to fight Paula Jones in court - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ready to fight Paula Jones in court - lawyer.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is ready to defend himself in court rather than apologise in the sexual harassment case that Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee, has brought against him, Clinton's personal lawyer said on Sunday.

Throwing down a gauntlet, the lawyer, Robert Bennett, said Clinton "is not going to apologise," one of three conditions for an out-of-court settlement established by Joseph Cammarata, a lawyer for Jones.

"I was listening to Mr. Cammarata last night, and the president of the United States is not going to apologise," Bennett said in an interview taped for one of a series of his scheduled television appearances on Sunday.

"And if she insists on a trial, we'll have a trial," Bennett added. "I notice a certain amount of cockiness out there, and as my mother once said to me, be careful what you wish for, you might get it."
He added: "So if they're insisting on proceeding, we'll proceed."

Cammarata, one of two lawyers representing Jones, said on Saturday night any settlement offer from Clinton would need to include "some sort of an apology," an affirmation of the truthfulness of Jones' account of what happened between her and the president and a statement exonerating her of any wrongdoing.
"Those are some minimal requirements that if those are not presented, this thing is dead in the water," Cammarata told CNN's "Inside Politics Weekend."

He also said he and Jones' other lawyer, Gil Davis, would recommend rejecting any settlement offer that did not include some financial renumeration for "the three years of hell that Paula Jones has been put through, the humiliation, the embarrassment, having her name just dragged through the mud."
Last week, the Supreme Court unanimously rejected Clinton's appeal for a delay in proceedings in Jones' suit until after he leaves office in 2000.

Jones contends that she took the legal action to clear her name after American Spectator published an article claiming that Arkansas state policemen set up sexual liaisons for Clinton when he was governor of Arkansas. One of the women in the article was identified by the name "Paula." Jones alleged this tied her to the case.
She alleged that Clinton made sexual advances to her in a Little Rock hotel room on May 8, 1991, including exposing himself to her and asking her to perform oral sex.
Clinton denies the allegations. The Supreme Court made no ruling on the merits of her case, but said a sitting president should be allowed to proceed.
